title: A monomorphism with a locally finite type composite is unramified and locally quasi-finite
statement: Let $X,Y,Z$ be schemes [def-pc-scheme] and let $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ be morphisms. Suppose $f$ is a monomorphism, meaning that $f\circ a=f\circ b$ implies $a=b$ for every scheme $T$ and morphisms $a,b:T\to X$, and suppose $g\circ f$ is locally of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Then $f$ is locally of finite type and its diagonal $\Delta_f:X\to X\times_YX$ [def-pc-fibre-product] is an isomorphism, hence both an open immersion [def-weil-open-immersion] and a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion]. In particular $f$ is separated [def-weil-proper-morphism] and unramified [def-weil-unramified-morphism]. Moreover $f$ is quasi-finite at every point in the affine-neighbourhood sense of [pqf-def-quasifinite] (1), and therefore locally quasi-finite in the sense of [pqf-def-quasifinite] (2). No quasi-compactness hypothesis on $X$ or separatedness hypothesis on $g$ is imposed.

source.place: Tags 01T8 (lemma-permanence-finite-type), 02GE (lemma-diagonal-unramified-morphism), and 02V5 (lemma-unramified-quasi-finite); diagonal argument: Schemes Tag 01L3 (lemma-monomorphism), with separatedness in 01L4 (lemma-monomorphism-separated). These give the general monomorphism argument used in Spaces Tag 0265, second proof paragraph.

proof.text: Apply clause (a) of [lemma-nagata-finite-type-to-separated-target] to the triangle $X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z$. Its sole hypothesis is that $g\circ f$ is locally of finite type, which is assumed. Thus $f$ is locally of finite type; no separatedness of $g$ or quasi-compactness is needed.

source.place: Tag 01T8, lemma-permanence-finite-type; the cancellation used in Spaces Tag 0265, second proof paragraph

proof.text: Put $P=X\times_YX$, with projections $p_1,p_2$, using [def-pc-fibre-product]. Their compatibility says $f\circ p_1=f\circ p_2$, so the monomorphism hypothesis gives $p_1=p_2$. The diagonal $\delta=(\mathrm{id}_X,\mathrm{id}_X)$ satisfies $p_1\circ\delta=\mathrm{id}_X$. Both projections of $\delta\circ p_1:P\to P$ agree with those of $\mathrm{id}_P$: they are $p_1$ and $p_1=p_2$. Uniqueness in the fibre-product universal property gives $\delta\circ p_1=\mathrm{id}_P$. Hence $\Delta_f=\delta$ is an isomorphism with inverse $p_1$.

source.place: Tag 01L3, lemma-monomorphism: categorical fibre-product argument written out

proof.text: An isomorphism is a homeomorphism onto the whole target, which is open and closed, and its structure-sheaf map is an isomorphism, hence surjective. Applying [def-weil-open-immersion] and [def-weil-closed-immersion] to $\Delta_f$ therefore makes it both an open and a closed immersion. Its being a closed immersion is precisely separatedness of $f$ by [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Together with step 1, its being an open immersion is precisely unramifiedness by [def-weil-unramified-morphism].

source.place: Tag 01L4, lemma-monomorphism-separated; unramifiedness: morphisms.tex Tag 02GE, lemma-diagonal-unramified-morphism (2)

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-unramified-quasi-finite-at-points] to the unramified morphism $f$ from step 3. Its statement gives, for every $x\in X$, affine neighbourhoods in $X$ and $Y$ on which the ring map is finite type and quasi-finite at the corresponding prime, exactly [pqf-def-quasifinite] (1). The same cited statement concludes local quasi-finiteness in sense (2). Thus all the asserted pointwise and local conclusions hold.
